The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice and use the negative-sign $2\pi$ normalization.  If
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\widehat f},$$

where $\widehat f$ is the integral Fourier transform.  If
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\mathcal F_2f},$$

where $\mathcal F_2$ is the Plancherel extension.  These equalities are in
$\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and therefore depend only on the corresponding
almost-everywhere classes.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

derivations.claim: For any real symmetric matrix $H$, maximize $z^{\mathsf T}Hz$ on the compact unit sphere. Differentiating along every tangent direction shows the maximizing vector is an eigenvector; its orthogonal complement is invariant under $H$, so induction gives an orthonormal eigenbasis. Applying this to $M$ constructs $M^{1/2}$ and $M^{-1/2}$. The condition $MA_j=A_j^{\mathsf T}M$ makes $\widetilde A_j=M^{1/2}A_jM^{-1/2}$ symmetric. Therefore each eigenvalue in $v_*$ is real and has absolute value at most $\sum_j\|\widetilde A_j\|$, so $v_*<\infty$. With $e=U^{\mathsf T}MU/2$ and $F_j=U^{\mathsf T}MA_jU/2$, the product rule gives $\partial_te+\sum_j\partial_{x_j}F_j=-U^{\mathsf T}SU\le0$ for every smooth solution, and $|F\cdot\nu|\le v_*e$ by diagonalizing $\widetilde A(\nu)$.

For Schwartz data, [F1] permits componentwise Fourier transformation of the system, giving $\partial_t\widehat U=C(\xi)\widehat U$ with $C(\xi)=-2\pi i\sum_j\xi_jA_j-B$. The matrix exponential $E(t,\xi)=e^{tC(\xi)}$, defined by its locally uniformly convergent power series, solves this finite-dimensional ODE. For $z(t)=E(t,\xi)z_0$, $\frac d{dt}(z^*Mz)=-2z^*Sz\le0$, because $MA(\xi)$ is real symmetric and its multiple by $-i$ has zero real quadratic part. Thus $\|E(t,\xi)\|_M\le1$ for $t\ge0$, uniformly in $\xi$; for $t<0$, $|\frac d{dt}(z^*Mz)|\le2\|M^{-1/2}SM^{-1/2}\|z^*Mz$, so Grönwall gives a uniform $e^{C|t|}$ bound on bounded time intervals.

Differentiating the matrix exponential with respect to $\xi_j$ gives $\partial_{\xi_j}E(t,\xi)=\int_0^tE(t-s,\xi)(-2\pi iA_j)E(s,\xi)\,ds$. Repeating this identity expresses every fixed $\xi$-derivative as a finite sum of ordered insertion integrals with constant matrix factors between evolution matrices. The uniform bounds from step 1.2 and the finite integration-simplex volumes bound each such derivative uniformly in $\xi$ on compact time intervals. Time derivatives multiply by $C(\xi)$ and therefore have at most polynomial growth in $\xi$. Leibniz's rule now shows $E(t,\cdot)\widehat U_0$ is Schwartz, uniformly in its seminorms on compact time intervals.

For periodic smooth data, integration by parts in a coordinate with maximal $|k_j|$ gives $|\widehat U_k(0)|\le C_N(1+|k|)^{-N}$ for every $N$. The series $U(t,x)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}e^{2\pi i k\cdot x/L}E(t,k/L)\widehat U_k(0)$ and every differentiated series converge uniformly on compact time intervals, by the same matrix-exponential derivative bounds and the lattice-shell estimate that a unit-width shell in $\mathbb Z^3$ has $O((1+r)^2)$ points. Hence it is a global smooth periodic solution and solves the PDE termwise. The modewise $M$-estimate from step 1.2 yields contraction of every weighted coefficient norm. For $s>3/2$, Cauchy–Schwarz and $M\ge\lambda_{\min}(M)I$ give $\sum_k|\widehat U_k(t)|\le\lambda_{\min}(M)^{-1/2}(\sum_k(1+|k/L|^2)^{-s})^{1/2}(\sum_k(1+|k/L|^2)^s\widehat U_k(t)^*M\widehat U_k(t))^{1/2}$; the first sum converges by the shell bound, proving the asserted uniform norm estimate. Integrating the equation against each periodic exponential shows that every solution coefficient solves the same finite-dimensional ODE, proving uniqueness.

Define $U(t)=\mathcal F^{-1}(E(t,\cdot)\widehat U_0)$. By [F2] this inverse is pointwise the absolutely convergent Fourier integral; the decay proved in step 2.1 permits every spatial and time derivative to pass under that integral, proves the PDE, and recovers $U(0)=U_0$. Conjugation symmetry of $C(\xi)$ and $\widehat U_0(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat U_0(\xi)}$ makes $U$ real.

By [F3] the Plancherel transform is unitary, and [F4] identifies it with the integral transform in $\mathcal S'$. Multiplying the pointwise $M$-norm estimate in step 1.2 by $(1+|\xi|^2)^s$ and integrating gives the stated $H^s_M$ contraction for every $s\ge0$.

Fix $t_*>0$, $x_*$, and $0\le t<t_*$. Put $R(t)=v_*(t_*-t)$ and $E(t)=\int_{B_{R(t)}(x_*)}e(t,x)\,dx$. In polar coordinates, the fundamental theorem of calculus differentiates this moving-ball integral; the PDE energy identity and [F5] then give $E'(t)=-\int_{\partial B_{R(t)}}(F\cdot\nu+v_*e)\,dS-\int_{B_{R(t)}}U^{\mathsf T}SU\,dx\le0$, since $|F\cdot\nu|\le v_*e$. If the initial data vanish on $B_{v_*t_*}(x_*)$, then $E(0)=0$; positivity of $M$ and $E(t)\ge0$ force $U(t,x_*)=0$ by continuity as $t\uparrow t_*$. For any $x$ with $|x-x_0|<R-v_*t_*$, the ball $B_{v_*t_*}(x)$ is contained in $B_R(x_0)$, proving the stated shrinking-ball conclusion. Applying the same argument to the difference of two solutions proves local uniqueness. Periodic lifts give the identical geodesic-ball conclusion on $\mathbb T_L^3$. If $v_*=0$, every symmetric $\widetilde A_j$ has zero spectrum and hence is zero, so each $A_j=0$; the pointwise ODE preserves spatial support.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$, let $\nabla$ be its metric-compatible torsion-free connection, and
let $u$ be a smooth future-directed vector field with $g(u,u)=-1$. Put
$\Delta^{ab}=g^{ab}+u^au^b$, $D=u^a\nabla_a$, $\theta=\nabla_a u^a$,
$a^b=u^a\nabla_a u^b$, and $\Delta^b{}_a=\delta^b{}_a+u^bu_a$.
Take a smooth fixed-composition state from [[def-tgr-local-fluid-state]] with
$n>0$, $T>0$, $s=n\sigma_p$, and $h=\epsilon+p=Ts+\mu n$ as in
[[lem-tgr-local-gibbs-euler]]. Define the perfect stress tensor and particle
current by

$$T^{ab}=\epsilon u^a u^b+p\Delta^{ab},\qquad J^a=nu^a.$$

For any smooth vector field $f^b$, the balance equation $\nabla_aT^{ab}=f^b$
is equivalent to the pair

$$D\epsilon+h\theta=-u_bf^b,\qquad ha^c+\Delta^{ca}\nabla_a p=\Delta^c{}_bf^b,$$

and $\nabla_aJ^a=0$ is equivalent to $Dn+n\theta=0$. Whenever both balances
hold, the exact entropy identities are

$$T\nabla_a(su^a)=-u_bf^b,\qquad nT D\sigma_p=-u_bf^b.$$

In particular, when $f=0$, the entropy current $su$ is divergence-free and
specific entropy is advected, $D\sigma_p=0$. These are conditional identities
for supplied smooth fields; they assert no solution existence or physical
applicability beyond the stated model data.

Let $X\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be nonempty and open, let $e\in C^2(X,\mathbb R)$, and define
$$Y:=\{(n,s)\in(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R:(1/n,s/n)\in X\},\qquad \varepsilon(n,s):=n\,e(1/n,s/n).$$
For $(n,s)\in Y$, put $v=1/n$, $\sigma_p=s/n$, $T=e_{\sigma_p}$, $p=-e_v$, $H=e+pv$, $h=\varepsilon+p=nH$, and $\mu=H-T\sigma_p$, as in [[def-tgr-local-fluid-state]]. Then the following identities hold as equalities of differentials on $Y$:
$$d\varepsilon=T\,ds+\mu\,dn,\qquad \varepsilon+p=Ts+\mu n,\qquad dp=s\,dT+n\,d\mu.$$

For parcel totals $\mathsf S\in\mathbb R$ (entropy), $\mathsf V>0$ (proper volume), and $\mathsf N>0$ (marker count) with $(\mathsf V/\mathsf N,\mathsf S/\mathsf N)\in X$, define
$$E(\mathsf S,\mathsf V,\mathsf N):=\mathsf N\,e(\mathsf V/\mathsf N,\mathsf S/\mathsf N).$$
Then $E$ is $C^2$, is positively homogeneous of degree one, and satisfies
$$dE=T\,d\mathsf S-p\,d\mathsf V+\mu\,d\mathsf N,\qquad E=T\mathsf S-p\mathsf V+\mu\mathsf N.$$
If $E$ is viewed on its open domain in $(\mathsf S,\mathsf V,\mathsf N)$, its Hessian annihilates the radial vector $(\mathsf S,\mathsf V,\mathsf N)$.

The local response statements are conditional. At a state with $T>0$ and $e_{\sigma_p\sigma_p}>0$, temperature is a valid local coordinate at fixed $v$, and the per-marker heat capacity
$$c_v:=\left(\frac{\partial e}{\partial T}\right)_v=\frac{T}{e_{\sigma_p\sigma_p}}$$
is positive. At a state with $e_{vv}>0$, the isentropic compressibility
$$\kappa_{\sigma_p}:=-\frac1v\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial p}\right)_{\sigma_p}=\frac1{v e_{vv}}$$
is positive. At a state with $e_{vv}>0$ and $h>0$, the local pressure-energy response
$$\alpha_{\sigma_p}:=\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial\varepsilon}\right)_{\sigma_p}=\frac{e_{vv}}{n h}$$
is positive. If $X$ is convex and $e$ is convex on $X$, then $D^2e$ is positive semidefinite. Positivity of the displayed diagonal responses is not asserted to imply convexity, a sound cone, or an evolution theorem.

Assume countable choice. Let $m\ge1$, let $U:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^m$, and let $A_1,A_2,A_3,B,M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be constant matrices. Assume $M=M^{\mathsf T}$ is positive definite, each $MA_j$ is symmetric, and $S:=(MB+B^{\mathsf T}M)/2$ is positive semidefinite. Consider

$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^3A_j\partial_{x_j}U+BU=0.$$

Use [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]: for $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and multi-indices $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N^3$, the scalar seminorm is $p_{\alpha\beta}(f):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^3}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$, and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$ consists of functions for which all these seminorms are finite. Here $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^m)$ means maps $U=(U_1,\ldots,U_m)$ with real-valued components such that each component, viewed as complex-valued with zero imaginary part, belongs to $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$; its vector seminorms are $p_{\alpha\beta}^{(m)}(U):=\max_{1\leq\ell\leq m}p_{\alpha\beta}(U_\ell)$. For $U_0\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^m)$ there is a unique global smooth solution, Schwartz in $x$ at each time and continuous in every $p_{\alpha\beta}^{(m)}$ on compact time intervals. With the negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform, put $\widehat U(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}U(x)\,dx$ and define, for $s\ge0$,

$$\|U\|_{H^s_M}^2:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|\xi|^2)^s\widehat U(\xi)^*M\widehat U(\xi)\,d\xi.$$

For $t\ge0$, $\|U(t)\|_{H^s_M}\le\|U_0\|_{H^s_M}$ for every $s\ge0$; hence the solution depends continuously on the data in each such norm. The same conclusions hold for smooth periodic data on the flat torus $\mathbb T_L^3:=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^3$, $L>0$, with Fourier coefficients $\widehat U_k=L^{-3}\int_{[0,L]^3}U(x)e^{-2\pi i k\cdot x/L}\,dx$ and

$$\|U\|_{H^s_M(\mathbb T_L^3)}^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k/L|^2)^s\widehat U_k^*M\widehat U_k.$$

For periodic data, $\|U(t)\|_\infty\le C_{s,L,M}\|U_0\|_{H^s_M(\mathbb T_L^3)}$ for each integer $s>3/2$.

For a unit vector $\nu\in\mathbb R^3$, write $A(\nu)=\sum_j\nu_jA_j$ and $\widetilde A(\nu)=M^{1/2}A(\nu)M^{-1/2}$. The finite speed

$$v_*:=\sup_{|\nu|=1}\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(\widetilde A(\nu))\}$$

is finite. If $v_*>0$, $R>v_*t$, and $U_0$ vanishes on $B_R(x_0)$, then $U(t)$ vanishes on $B_{R-v_*t}(x_0)$ for $0\le t<R/v_*$. The same assertion holds on $\mathbb T_L^3$ using its geodesic distance. If $v_*=0$, every $A_j=0$ and the system is a pointwise linear ODE, so spatial support does not move. These are conclusions for the displayed linear systems; no variable-coefficient or nonlinear existence claim is included.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

derivations.claim: The family is normalized by $\eta(u_\lambda,u_\lambda)=-1$ and is future-directed, so at $\lambda=0$ it has $u_0=\bar u$ and differentiating normalization gives $\delta u^0=0$. Since $\partial_0=c^{-1}\partial_t$, the first variation of $D\epsilon$ is $c^{-1}r_t$, that of $\theta$ is $\operatorname{div}w$, and that of the spatial acceleration is $c^{-1}\partial_t w$. By [F2], $\delta p=a_s r$ and $\delta n=(n_0/h_0)r$. Taking first variations of the energy and spatial equations in [F1] therefore gives $r_t+c h_0\operatorname{div}w=0$ and $w_t+(c a_s/h_0)\nabla r=0$; the particle equation follows from $\delta n=(n_0/h_0)r$ and the first equation.

Put $U=(r,w)$ and $M=\operatorname{diag}(a_s/h_0,h_0I_3)$. The matrix $M$ is positive definite because $a_s,h_0>0$. For each $j$, define $A_j$ by $(A_j)_{r,w_j}=ch_0$, $(A_j)_{w_j,r}=ca_s/h_0$, with all other entries zero. Then $MA_j$ is symmetric. In a unit direction $
u$, the longitudinal block of $A(
u)$ on $(r,w\cdot
u)$ has eigenvalues $\pm c\sqrt{a_s}$ and the two transverse components have eigenvalue $0$. Thus [F3] constructs the actual global smooth solution and yields its uniqueness, contraction, and propagation speed $c\sqrt{a_s}$.

Direct multiplication of the equations by $(a_s/h_0)r$ and $h_0w$ gives $\partial_t\mathcal E+\operatorname{div}(c a_s r w)=0$. For a unit normal $\nu$, $|c a_s r\,w\cdot\nu|\le c\sqrt{a_s}\,\mathcal E$ by $2XY\le X^2+Y^2$ with $X=\sqrt{a_s/h_0}|r|$ and $Y=\sqrt{h_0}|w|$. Since $0<a_s\le1$, this flux cone lies inside the reference cone of speed $c$.

Under the formal coefficient convention [A3], for $k\ne0$ and $a_s>0$, $r=A\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t)$, $w=(\omega A/(c h_0|k|^2))k\cos(k\cdot x-\omega t)$ solves both equations when $\omega^2=c^2a_s|k|^2$; substitution gives both equalities. Hence $a_s>1$ has exact modes with speed greater than $c$. If $a_s<0$, put $\lambda=c\sqrt{-a_s}|k|$ and take $r=Ae^{\lambda t}\cos(k\cdot x)$, $w=-(\lambda A/(c h_0|k|^2))k e^{\lambda t}\sin(k\cdot x)$; differentiating verifies both equations and gives unbounded growth rates as $|k|\to\infty$. At $a_s=0$ the weight $a_s/h_0$ vanishes, so the positive-definite argument in step 2.1 is inapplicable.

$(-,+,+,+)$, let $\nabla$ be its metric-compatible torsion-free connection, and
let $u$ be a smooth future-directed vector field with $g(u,u)=-1$. Put
$\Delta^{ab}=g^{ab}+u^au^b$, $D=u^a\nabla_a$, $\theta=\nabla_a u^a$,

[[lem-tgr-local-gibbs-euler]]. Define the perfect stress tensor and particle
current by

$$T^{ab}=\epsilon u^a u^b+p\Delta^{ab},\qquad J^a=nu^a.$$

is equivalent to the pair

$$D\epsilon+h\theta=-u_bf^b,\qquad ha^c+\Delta^{ca}\nabla_a p=\Delta^c{}_bf^b,$$

$$T\nabla_a(su^a)=-u_bf^b,\qquad nT D\sigma_p=-u_bf^b.$$

Let $X\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be nonempty and open, let $e\in C^2(X,\mathbb R)$, and define
$$Y:=\{(n,s)\in(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R:(1/n,s/n)\in X\},\qquad \varepsilon(n,s):=n\,e(1/n,s/n).$$
For $(n,s)\in Y$, put $v=1/n$, $\sigma_p=s/n$, $T=e_{\sigma_p}$, $p=-e_v$, $H=e+pv$, $h=\varepsilon+p=nH$, and $\mu=H-T\sigma_p$, as in [[def-tgr-local-fluid-state]]. Then the following identities hold as equalities of differentials on $Y$:
$$d\varepsilon=T\,ds+\mu\,dn,\qquad \varepsilon+p=Ts+\mu n,\qquad dp=s\,dT+n\,d\mu.$$

For parcel totals $\mathsf S\in\mathbb R$ (entropy), $\mathsf V>0$ (proper volume), and $\mathsf N>0$ (marker count) with $(\mathsf V/\mathsf N,\mathsf S/\mathsf N)\in X$, define
$$E(\mathsf S,\mathsf V,\mathsf N):=\mathsf N\,e(\mathsf V/\mathsf N,\mathsf S/\mathsf N).$$
Then $E$ is $C^2$, is positively homogeneous of degree one, and satisfies
$$dE=T\,d\mathsf S-p\,d\mathsf V+\mu\,d\mathsf N,\qquad E=T\mathsf S-p\mathsf V+\mu\mathsf N.$$
If $E$ is viewed on its open domain in $(\mathsf S,\mathsf V,\mathsf N)$, its Hessian annihilates the radial vector $(\mathsf S,\mathsf V,\mathsf N)$.

The local response statements are conditional. At a state with $T>0$ and $e_{\sigma_p\sigma_p}>0$, temperature is a valid local coordinate at fixed $v$, and the per-marker heat capacity
$$c_v:=\left(\frac{\partial e}{\partial T}\right)_v=\frac{T}{e_{\sigma_p\sigma_p}}$$
is positive. At a state with $e_{vv}>0$, the isentropic compressibility
$$\kappa_{\sigma_p}:=-\frac1v\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial p}\right)_{\sigma_p}=\frac1{v e_{vv}}$$
is positive. At a state with $e_{vv}>0$ and $h>0$, the local pressure-energy response
$$\alpha_{\sigma_p}:=\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial\varepsilon}\right)_{\sigma_p}=\frac{e_{vv}}{n h}$$
is positive. If $X$ is convex and $e$ is convex on $X$, then $D^2e$ is positive semidefinite. Positivity of the displayed diagonal responses is not asserted to imply convexity, a sound cone, or an evolution theorem.

Assume countable choice. Let $m\ge1$, let $U:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^m$, and let $A_1,A_2,A_3,B,M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be constant matrices. Assume $M=M^{\mathsf T}$ is positive definite, each $MA_j$ is symmetric, and $S:=(MB+B^{\mathsf T}M)/2$ is positive semidefinite. Consider

$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^3A_j\partial_{x_j}U+BU=0.$$

Use [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]: for $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and multi-indices $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N^3$, the scalar seminorm is $p_{\alpha\beta}(f):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^3}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$, and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$ consists of functions for which all these seminorms are finite. Here $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^m)$ means maps $U=(U_1,\ldots,U_m)$ with real-valued components such that each component, viewed as complex-valued with zero imaginary part, belongs to $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$; its vector seminorms are $p_{\alpha\beta}^{(m)}(U):=\max_{1\leq\ell\leq m}p_{\alpha\beta}(U_\ell)$. For $U_0\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^m)$ there is a unique global smooth solution, Schwartz in $x$ at each time and continuous in every $p_{\alpha\beta}^{(m)}$ on compact time intervals. With the negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform, put $\widehat U(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}U(x)\,dx$ and define, for $s\ge0$,

$$\|U\|_{H^s_M}^2:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|\xi|^2)^s\widehat U(\xi)^*M\widehat U(\xi)\,d\xi.$$

For $t\ge0$, $\|U(t)\|_{H^s_M}\le\|U_0\|_{H^s_M}$ for every $s\ge0$; hence the solution depends continuously on the data in each such norm. The same conclusions hold for smooth periodic data on the flat torus $\mathbb T_L^3:=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^3$, $L>0$, with Fourier coefficients $\widehat U_k=L^{-3}\int_{[0,L]^3}U(x)e^{-2\pi i k\cdot x/L}\,dx$ and

$$\|U\|_{H^s_M(\mathbb T_L^3)}^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k/L|^2)^s\widehat U_k^*M\widehat U_k.$$

For periodic data, $\|U(t)\|_\infty\le C_{s,L,M}\|U_0\|_{H^s_M(\mathbb T_L^3)}$ for each integer $s>3/2$.

For a unit vector $\nu\in\mathbb R^3$, write $A(\nu)=\sum_j\nu_jA_j$ and $\widetilde A(\nu)=M^{1/2}A(\nu)M^{-1/2}$. The finite speed

$$v_*:=\sup_{|\nu|=1}\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(\widetilde A(\nu))\}$$

is finite. If $v_*>0$, $R>v_*t$, and $U_0$ vanishes on $B_R(x_0)$, then $U(t)$ vanishes on $B_{R-v_*t}(x_0)$ for $0\le t<R/v_*$. The same assertion holds on $\mathbb T_L^3$ using its geodesic distance. If $v_*=0$, every $A_j=0$ and the system is a pointwise linear ODE, so spatial support does not move. These are conclusions for the displayed linear systems; no variable-coefficient or nonlinear existence claim is included.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
